name: Tamper Evidence
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Tamper Evident Is Not the Same as Tamper Proof
lesson.summary: Tamper evidence means unauthorized changes leave a detectable trace, not that changes are impossible, and hash chains and Merkle trees are what make that trace visible.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to hear that a system uses cryptographic hashing and assume the data inside it cannot be changed. That is the wrong mental model, and it matters for a skeptical reading of any trust technology. Tamper proof would mean a change is physically or mathematically impossible to make. Tamper evident means something weaker and more honest: a change can be made, but making it leaves behind a detectable inconsistency that a verifier can find. Hash chains and Merkle trees are tamper evident structures, not tamper proof ones.

The mechanism should already feel familiar from the previous two chapters. In a hash chain, editing an old record changes its hash, which no longer matches the hash embedded in the next record, which in turn breaks every subsequent link. In a Merkle tree, editing a leaf changes its hash, which propagates up and changes the root. In both cases, nothing stops a person with write access to the underlying storage from actually editing the bytes. What the structure guarantees is that if they do, the recomputed hashes will disagree with the previously recorded ones, and anyone who checks will see the mismatch.

This is a meaningful upgrade over ordinary data integrity checking, which typically answers a narrower question: does this one file match its last known checksum. Tamper evidence, built from chained or tree structured hashes, answers a broader question across a whole history: is this entire sequence or set still internally consistent with itself. A single unauthorized edit anywhere does not just corrupt one record, it becomes visible as a structural break relative to everything that depends on it.

Consider a concrete case. A company keeps an internal audit log of who accessed a sensitive database, with each entry chained to the last. An employee with database access edits an old log entry to hide an unauthorized query. The edit itself is easy to make, nothing in the storage layer prevents writing new bytes over old ones. But the moment anyone recomputes the chain from the beginning and compares it to a previously published or externally stored tip hash, the discrepancy appears. The tampering is now evident, even though it was not prevented.

That last detail, an externally stored or independently witnessed tip hash, is what makes tamper evidence actually useful rather than theoretical. If the only copy of the chain's final hash lives in the same system an attacker already compromised, they can simply recompute and overwrite that hash too, erasing the evidence along with the tampering. Real tamper evident systems address this by publishing tips widely, distributing copies across independent parties, or anchoring them somewhere harder to alter, which is exactly the problem that distributed and decentralized structures, covered later in this book, are built to solve at scale.
